title: Nehemiah 7:61–73
context: Some returnees could not prove their descent, and certain priestly families were excluded from the priesthood until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim. Both lists give the same total of 42,360 (Nehemiah 7:66; Ezra 2:64), though the listed groups in each add up to less than that total, and interpreters explain the gap differently. Nehemiah then records gifts for the work that differ in amount and arrangement from Ezra 2:68-69, and closes with the people settled in their towns as the seventh month arrives, leading into the reading of the law in chapter 8.

verses.text: These were those who went up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer; but they could not show their fathers’ houses, nor their offspring, whether they were of Israel:
verses.arminianNotes: Some came from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer but could not prove their descent. Arminian readers see people who chose to join the return despite uncertainty about their status.
verses.reformedNotes: Ezra 2:59 reads Addan instead of Addon. Reformed readers note that these places were probably in Babylonia, though their locations are unknown, and that the issue is lineage, not sincerity.

verses.text: The children of Delaiah, the children of Tobiah, the children of Nekoda: six hundred forty-two.
verses.arminianNotes: The children of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda: six hundred forty-two, where Ezra 2:60 has six hundred fifty-two. Arminian readers note that these families were still counted among the returnees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see their inclusion, despite uncertain descent, as evidence that the community was not closed to them. Their status was unclear, but they were not sent away.

verses.text: Of the priests: the children of Hobaiah, the children of Hakkoz, the children of Barzillai, who took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name.
verses.arminianNotes: Of the priests: Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, who took his name from his wife’s family. Ezra 2:61 spells the first name Habaiah. Arminian readers see families whose standing rested on records now lost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Barzillai the Gileadite had supported David during Absalom’s revolt (2 Samuel 17:27-29; 19:31-39). Taking that honored name may have obscured the priestly line.

verses.text: These searched for their genealogical records, but couldn’t find them. Therefore they were deemed disqualified and removed from the priesthood.
verses.arminianNotes: They searched for their records but could not find them and were excluded from the priesthood. Arminian readers see the seriousness with which the community guarded holy service, even at personal cost.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the law restricted priesthood to Aaron’s descendants (Numbers 3:10; 16:40). The exclusion reflects faithfulness to God’s command, not hostility toward these families.

verses.text: The governor told them not to eat of the most holy things until a priest stood up to minister with Urim and Thummim.
verses.arminianNotes: The governor forbade them the most holy things until a priest arose with Urim and Thummim. Arminian readers see a provisional ruling that left room for God to settle the question later.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Urim and Thummim were means of discerning God’s will (Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21), though how they worked is unknown and there is no clear record of their use after the exile.

verses.text: The whole assembly together was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty,
verses.arminianNotes: The whole assembly was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty, the same total as Ezra 2:64. Arminian readers observe that in both books the groups listed individually add up to less than this figure.
verses.reformedNotes: Added together, the listed groups come to thirty-one thousand eighty-nine in Nehemiah and twenty-nine thousand eight hundred eighteen in Ezra. Reformed readers note that interpreters explain the gap in several ways; the agreed total is shared ground.

verses.text: in addition to their male servants and their female servants, of whom there were seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven. They had two hundred forty-five singing men and singing women.
verses.arminianNotes: Besides seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven servants, there were two hundred forty-five singers. Ezra 2:65 gives two hundred singing men and women. Arminian readers see music woven into the life of the returnees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the number of servants matches Ezra exactly, while the singers differ by forty-five. The presence of singing men and women shows praise accompanying the community.

verses.text: Their horses were seven hundred thirty-six; their mules, two hundred forty-five;
verses.arminianNotes: Their horses were seven hundred thirty-six and their mules two hundred forty-five, matching Ezra 2:66. Arminian readers see a modest caravan, the means of a people rebuilding with limited resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the figures for horses and mules agree with Ezra. The list of animals shows the practical side of the long journey from Babylon.

verses.text: their camels, four hundred thirty-five; their donkeys, six thousand seven hundred twenty.
verses.arminianNotes: Their camels were four hundred thirty-five and their donkeys six thousand seven hundred twenty, matching Ezra 2:67. Arminian readers note that donkeys far outnumber other animals, suited to carrying loads.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the full agreement in the animal counts contrasts with variations in the family figures. The record is careful throughout but not uniform in every detail.

verses.text: Some from among the heads of fathers’ households gave to the work. The governor gave to the treasury one thousand darics of gold, fifty basins, and five hundred thirty priests’ garments.
verses.arminianNotes: Some heads of households gave to the work; the governor gave a thousand darics of gold, fifty basins, and five hundred thirty priests’ garments. Arminian readers see leaders setting an example of generosity.
verses.reformedNotes: Ezra 2:68-69 records the gifts as one sum from the heads of households, without separating the governor’s share. Reformed readers note that Nehemiah’s arrangement differs, and the amounts follow in the next verses.

verses.text: Some of the heads of fathers’ households gave into the treasury of the work twenty thousand darics of gold, and two thousand two hundred minas of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: Some heads of households gave twenty thousand darics of gold and two thousand two hundred minas of silver. Arminian readers see willing giving from those with means, a response to the work at hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah’s three gifts total forty-one thousand darics, four thousand two hundred minas, and five hundred ninety-seven garments, while Ezra 2:69 records sixty-one thousand darics, five thousand minas, and one hundred garments.

verses.text: That which the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand darics of gold, plus two thousand minas of silver, and sixty-seven priests’ garments.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest of the people added an equal sum in gold, two thousand minas of silver, and sixty-seven priests’ garments. Arminian readers see ordinary people sharing in the work alongside their leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see generosity spread across the whole community, not limited to the wealthy. The differences from Ezra’s totals are named here but left unreconciled, as with the family figures.

verses.text: So the priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all Israel lived in their cities. When the seventh month had come, the children of Israel were in their cities.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests, Levites, and all Israel lived in their towns, and the seventh month came. Arminian readers see a settled people ready to gather, as the next chapter shows, to hear the law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the closing words closely resemble Ezra 2:70 and Ezra 3:1. The settlement leads into the public reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:1-2), where restoration turns from walls to the word of God.
